extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, graduate students, and informed readers interested in analytic number theory and prime gaps
extracted.subtask_description: An expository account of Yitang Zhang's proof that there are infinitely many pairs of primes with difference < 70 million, explaining the GPY framework, notions like admissible tuples and level of distribution, and Zhang's modifications to the Selberg sieve and error-term analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible tuple
rubrics_metrics.description: A tuple without the obstruction that some prime always divides one of its components is called admissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (n,n+1) is only a prime tuple for (2,3) since one of n or n+1 is even; (n,n+2,n+4) only for (3,5,7) because one component is divisible by 3. Tuples like (n,n+2) and (n,n+2,n+6) have no such obstruction and are expected to be prime tuples infinitely often. The admissibility condition is a necessary combinatorial constraint when searching for prime tuples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selberg sieve produces 'almost prime' tuples
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Selberg sieve to a k-tuple over n ≤ x to remove tuples where any component has a small prime factor, leaving tuples where components have only large prime factors — 'almost prime' tuples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roughly: the sieve removes tuples with small prime divisors, so the remaining tuples have relatively few prime factors distributed among components. For instance, a 10-tuple where the components together have at most 18 prime factors would force at least two components to be prime. The Selberg sieve is effective at producing almost-prime tuples but cannot alone detect primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freezing/twisting a component to detect primes
rubrics_metrics.description: Freeze (or twist) one component of the tuple to be a prime and count how often that frozen prime component occurs among the almost-prime tuples produced by the sieve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the proportion of almost-prime tuples where a given component is prime by counting in arithmetic progressions determined by the divisors used in sieving. Freeze each component individually; if the amount when freezing one component exceeds 1/k times the total contribution of all almost-prime tuples, overlaps must occur and two components are simultaneously prime, producing a prime pair within the tuple.

rubrics_metrics.name: GPY success criterion via level of distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The GPY method yields bounded gaps between primes provided the primes have level of distribution θ > 1/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If θ > 1/2 then for sufficiently large k the method produces two primes in the tuple. With only known level θ = 1/2 (Bombieri–Vinogradov) GPY does not unconditionally produce two primes in any fixed tuple; improving the level of distribution is the key barrier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of distribution (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If almost all arithmetic progressions modulo q with q up to x^α satisfy the prime number theorem in progressions, then the primes have level of distribution θ where θ > α; the primes are conjectured to have level 1 (Elliott–Halberstam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bombieri–Vinogradov proves the asymptotic for 'almost all' q up to x^{1/2}, giving level θ = 1/2 for many applications. Under GRH one gets the asymptotic for any α < 1/2 but GRH does not imply a level > 1/2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliott–Halberstam implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming Elliott–Halberstam (primes have level of distribution 1) yields two primes infinitely often in every admissible 6-tuple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: the smallest admissible 6-tuple (n, n+4, n+6, n+10, n+12, n+16) would give prime pairs with difference ≤ 16. This is a conditional improvement compared to what is known unconditionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem role
rubrics_metrics.description: Bombieri–Vinogradov shows the asymptotic formula for primes in arithmetic progressions holds for almost all q up to x^{1/2}, giving level of distribution 1/2 for many applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For many applications that average over many progressions, Bombieri–Vinogradov has the same strength as GRH. However, level 1/2 is insufficient for GPY to obtain bounded prime gaps unconditionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of older improvements (BFI methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Results of Bombieri, Friedlander, and Iwaniec (and others) go beyond level 1/2 in certain weighted-sum contexts, sometimes corresponding to an effective level like 4/7, but they apply to weighted sums rather than absolute value sums of error terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods rely on spectral theory of automorphic forms and provide powerful tools for weighted error terms. In GPY context, previous attempts could not use these techniques to control the specific error terms generated by the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zhang's sieve modification (no large prime factors and extended range)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict the Selberg sieve to divisors with no large prime factors (which decreases sieve effectiveness) and simultaneously increase the sieving range corresponding to a level of distribution 1/2 + 1/584; then control error terms via intricate analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: removing large-prime divisors reduces effectiveness but only slightly; divisors without large prime factors can be factored into factors of various sizes providing flexibility; the increased effective sieving range (1/2 + 1/584) is enough to overcome the loss and give bounded gaps provided all error terms are controlled using Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec style techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error-term control via BFI-style analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: To make Zhang's modification work one must control many intricate error terms, employing methods from Bombieri, Friedlander, and Iwaniec involving spectral theory and estimates for weighted sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crucial importance is that the sieving divisors have no large prime factors, enabling factorizations and flexible weightings; the analysis shows all error terms are controlled leading to the final result. It's noted this does not prove the primes themselves have level of distribution > 1/2 by the standard definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of k and tuple width (quantitative output)
rubrics_metrics.description: Zhang proves every admissible k-tuple with k = 3,500,000 contains 2 primes, which leads to a bound on gaps (width of a chosen admissible tuple) of about 70,000,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specific number (70 million) arises from a convenient choice of shifts (e.g., first k primes larger than k) and rounding for simplicity; the numerical bound has no intrinsic significance and is expected to be reducible by further refinements.
